litw-study-subtitle: Make sure to quickly present your study and tell participants what they will get out of it!
litw-study-description-p1: Welcome! This LabintheWild test will tell you what kind of decision-making style you have and how this compares to other people across the globe.
litw-study-description-p2: The test typically takes 5 minutes to complete.
litw-irb2-header: Before we get started, here are a few things you should know...
litw-irb2-q1: What is this study all about?
litw-irb2-a1-p1: In this study, you'll be able to find out how your cultural background influences how you use and see technology. By doing this research, we hope to improve access to digital technology for diverse people. Our research is supported by the National Science Foundation.
litw-irb2-a1-p2: We’ll ask you questions about your demographics, experiences, and about your decision-making. You can then see how you compare to other people around the world! Altogether, this will take around
litw-irb2-q2: What data are we going to collect?
litw-irb2-a2: We will not collect your name and contact information. However, we will collect the city and country you are located in, what browser you are using, your answers to our questions, and data about how you use our website. We will securely store this data.
litw-irb2-q3: Do I have to be in this study?
litw-irb2-a3: No, being in this study is up to you. You can leave now or at any time later.
litw-irb2-q4: Who you can contact if you have questions?
litw-irb2-a4-p1: If you have questions or concerns, you may contact Professor Katharina Reinecke, Paul G. Allen Center for Computer Science & Engineering, Box 352350, Seattle, WA 98195, reinecke@cs.washington.edu.
litw-irb2-a4-p2: If you want to talk about the study with someone who is not part of the study team, contact the University of Washington Human Subjects Division at: hsdinfo@uw.edu or 206.543.0098. (for international calls include the US Calling Code: +1-206-543-0098).

litw-study-intervention-UNIQUE-body: The patterns in your data reflect your own individual decision-making style, influenced by your culture, upbringing and experiences. As you complete this test, you'll be contributing a unique data point that only you can provide.

litw-results-box-title: Here is what the different decision-making styles mean
litw-results-vigilance-explanation: Vigilance: A vigilant decision maker often takes time to think carefully before making choices, they do not rush into things without thinking, instead, they pay attention to details and consider the possible outcomes.
litw-results-hypervigilance-explanation: Hypervigilance: The decision maker who is hyper-vigilant or panicky tends to search urgently for solutions when confronted with dilemmas. They may act impulsively, grabbing quick fixes that seem to offer relief from conflicts.
litw-results-buckpassing-explanation: Buckpassing: This decision maker often evades responsibility by shifting decisions to others, resulting in delayed actions and reduced initiative.
litw-results-procrastination-explanation: Procrastination: This decision maker attempts to escape difficult decisions by procrastinating or constructing wishful rationalizations to justify the least objectionable alternative.
litw-results-dmselfesteem-explanation: Decision Self-Esteem: An individual's decision self esteem refers to how they feel about their personal competence as a decision maker.
litw-results-paper-info1: * Note: The data for this study is based on the paper 'Cross-cultural differences in self-reported decision-making style and confidence'.
litw-results-paper-info2: Decision-making styles refer to an individual’s preferred approach to making choices and decisions. We based this study on the Melbourne Decision Making Questionnaire developed by Leon Mann [cite]. Here are the decision-making styles he found:
litw-results-paper-citation: Mann, L., Radford, M., Burnett, P., Ford, S., Bond, M., Leung, K., Nakamura, H., Vaughan, G., & Yang, K.-S.(1998). Cross-cultural differences in self-reported decision-making style and confidence. International Journal of Psychology, 33(5), 325–335.

study-mann-expl1: To what extent are the following statements true for you?
study-mann-q1: I like to consider all of the alternatives.
study-mann-q2: I try to find out the disadvantages of all alternatives.
study-mann-q3: I consider how best to carry out a decision.
study-mann-q4: When making decisions I like to collect a lot of information.
study-mann-q5: I try to be clear about my objectives before choosing.
study-mann-q6: I take a lot of care before choosing.
study-mann-q8: I do not make decisions unless I really have to.
study-mann-q9: I prefer to leave decisions to others.
study-mann-q10: I do not like to take responsibility for making decisions.
study-mann-q11: If a decision can be made by me or another person I let the other person make it.
study-mann-q12: I prefer that people who are better informed decide for me.
study-mann-q13: Whenever I face a difficult decision I feel pessimistic about finding a good solution.
study-mann-q14: I feel as if I am under tremendous time pressure when making decisions.
study-mann-q15: The possibility that some small thing might go wrong causes me to swing abruptly in my preference.
study-mann-q16: I cannot think straight if I have to make a decision in a hurry.
study-mann-q17: After a decision is made I spend a lot of time convincing myself it was correct.
study-mann-q18: I waste a lot of time on trivial matters before getting to the final decision.
study-mann-q19: Even after I have made a decision I delay acting upon it.
study-mann-q20: When I have to make a decision I wait a long time before starting to think about it.
study-mann-q21: I delay making decisions until it is too late.
study-mann-q23: I feel confident about my ability to make decisions.
study-mann-q24: I feel inferior to most people in making decisions.
study-mann-q25: I think that I am a good decision maker.
study-mann-q26: I feel so discouraged that I give up trying to make decisions.
study-mann-q27: The decisions I make turn out well.
study-mann-q28: It is easy for other people to convince me that their decision rather than mine is the correct one.
